newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FUND VIEW-Asset managers say scared of S.E. Asia.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Asset managers say scared of S.E. Asia.

text.p: International fund managers said on Friday they would continue withdrawing from Southeast Asia in the near term, seeking to cut their losses after the currency devaluations in the Philippines and Thailand.

They told Reuters at a fund managers' conference that their exit from countries such as Malaysia and the Philippines were fundamentally unwarranted, but the pressure of speculators selling the region's currencies was too strong to ignore.

"We are a little frightened right now. The immediate reaction is to stay out of ASEAN (the Association of South East Asian Nations)," said Lynda Couch, senior vice-president, portfolio management, at U.S. firm Newport Pacific Management.
"Some of us are stepping back for a while, hoping there will be better value to buy into soon," she said.
She added the selling of the region was triggered by big hedge funds, which are basically speculative in nature. "Regular investors have been frightened off (by speculators)," she said.
Withdrawals of funds from Southeast Asian countries over the past three months have sharply pulled down their stock markets.

The announcement of a banking industry crisis in Thailand due to its over-exposure to the troubled property sector accelerated disinvestment from the region, whose stock markets have grown mainly on foreign investment pumped in over the past few years.
Fund managers said they were concerned about the property sector problems in the region, but the reasons were not compelling enough except in Thailand.
In addition, most Asian economies are running huge current account deficits and many of them were being funded through short-term rather than long-term funds.
"I think people have been concerned about the quality of financial assets (of countries in the region)," said Edward Goodchild, fund manager with Foreign & Colonial Emerging Markets Ltd in London.
"But, it is not as if everybody is in the same position. And central banks of the region have heeded the warning and are doing something about it," he added.
However, Goodchild said the withdrawals were temporary and funds would return to the region before too long.
"There is market turbulence. I don't believe there will be a domino effect across Asia," he said. "Also, I don't think any ASEAN currencies are under any significant long-term threat."
He said his company was currently underweight Asia and overweight Latin America. "In Asia we are most bullish about Hong Kong," he said.
A vice-president of equities risk management at a European fund manager said investors were moving to north Asia for better returns.
"Funds are going to North Asia, Greater China, Hong Kong, the red-chips in particular, and Taiwan, where companies are enjoying high levels of global growth," he said.
Red chips are Hong Kong-incorporated companies with financial backing from China.

The fund manager added that most Western funds had high levels of exposure to property and finance stocks in the region since they were among the biggest capitalised. "You don't have many manufacturing companies here that are big enough and liquid," he said.
